title: Finite-Syndrome Compression of Quantum Fisher Information
abstract: Readable error records can protect quantum sensing because they prevent physically distinct noise trajectories from being irreversibly mixed. A finite detector or ancilla, however, can retain only finitely many syndrome values, and a general criterion for deciding which records may be merged without losing metrological information is absent. We formulate the problem for a fixed fine-grained classical-quantum record and parameter-independent compression into at most $M$ flags. We prove an exact identity expressing the lost symmetric-logarithmic-derivative quantum Fisher information (SLD QFI) as a sum of state-weighted squared distances between fine and coarse SLD scores. Consequently, optimal finite-syndrome design is exactly an operator-valued clustering problem, and zero loss is characterized by a support-resolved common-SLD condition. We extend the identity to the full multiparameter SLD QFI matrix and distinguish local QFI preservation from recovery of an entire statistical model. For exact recovery of a quantum code, we separately show that, when each fine error is individually correctable, the minimum number of readable syndromes is the chromatic number of a Knill-Laflamme incompatibility graph. For qubit random-unitary noise we obtain a finite partition formula. A planar random-Pauli model admits a conditional-variance representation and, for a uniform error axis, the exact optimum $F_M^{\star}=[M\sin(π/M)/π]^2$, with deficit $π^2/(3M^2)+O(M^{-4})$. These results identify the information-theoretic cost of finite syndrome resolution while making explicit the side-information assumptions required for any passive noise-to-erasure interpretation.
summary: This theoretical paper quantifies the fundamental trade-off between measurement resolution and achievable quantum sensing precision. It proves an exact identity showing that QFI loss due to syndrome compression equals a measurable mismatch between fine and coarse information estimates. The results establish necessary conditions for lossless encoding, linking it to graph theory (chromatic number) in code settings.
main_problem: The paper addresses how much Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) is unavoidably lost when compressing a fine-grained quantum measurement record into a finite set of measurable syndrome flags.
main_result: It derives an exact identity quantifying this QFI loss, showing that optimal compression is equivalent to solving an operator-valued clustering problem.
method: The authors use the Symmetric-Logarithmic-Derivative (SLD) Quantum Fisher Information as a diagnostic tool and establish variational principles relating the achievable QFI to squared distances between fine and coarse SLD scores.
model_or_system: The analysis is general, focusing on quantum sensing protocols where noise creates distinguishable but observationally mixed trajectories. Specific models include qubit random-unitary noise and planar random-Pauli axes.
key_observables: Symmetric-Logarithmic-Derivative Quantum Fisher Information (SLD QFI), the minimum number of readable syndromes ($\chi(G_P)$), and the QFI deficit ($D_M$).
important_parameters: The finite number of syndrome flags, $M$, which dictates the compression level.
main_assumptions: The analysis fixes the fine-grained record and assumes parameter-independent classical compression; it also notes that SLD preservation is a local condition weaker than full statistical model recovery.
figures_summary: Not specified in the provided notes, but the structure implies mathematical derivations leading to explicit formulas for QFI loss (e.g., $F_M^{\star}=[M\sin(\pi/M)/\pi]^2$).
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing an exact identity quantifying QFI loss due to finite syndrome resolution, showing this maps the problem to operator-valued clustering. It then applies this framework to specific physical models (e.g., quantum codes, planar axes) to derive concrete bounds and necessary conditions for lossless compression.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous information-theoretic bounds on sensing precision when measurement resources are limited, which is crucial for designing practical quantum sensors that must operate with finite detectors.
